title: Global History 9 ENL
subtitle: Words first, then the world
note: A review site for Global History 9 ENL. Every unit starts with its key words in English, Pinyin, Chinese, and Spanish, then the lessons in the order we teach them. Study help only. No answers here.

units.title: Course Launch
units.blurb: Two opening days where you meet the class, read the course outline in English, Chinese, and Spanish, and draw a world map from memory.

lessons.title: Course launch + expectations
lessons.overview: What is history, how is it different from 'the past,' and why do historians ask questions before they trust a source?
objectives: I can EXPLAIN what history is and DESCRIBE how a historian reads a source, using key vocabulary and sentence starters.

lessons.title: Social Pyramid (about-you) + draw map from memory
lessons.overview: What habits do historians use to read a source carefully and decide what it can prove?
objectives: I can DESCRIBE the habits historians use and EXPLAIN how they read one source, using key vocabulary and sentence starters.

units.title: Geography

units.title: Paleolithic and Neolithic
units.blurb: How people moved from hunting and gathering to farming, and why growing food in one place changed everything.

lessons.title: From Hunter to Farmer notes (Paleo vs Neo)
lessons.overview: What choices did a hunter-gatherer band have to make to survive when food was scarce?
objectives: I can EXPLAIN the choices a hunter-gatherer band made to survive and DESCRIBE how scarcity affected them, using key vocabulary and sentence starters.

lessons.title: Paleo/Neo Vocab Review do-now
lessons.overview: How did learning to farm change human life from moving bands into settled villages?
objectives: I can EXPLAIN what the Neolithic Revolution was and DESCRIBE how farming changed human life, using key vocabulary and sentence starters.

lessons.title: Neolithic Revolution reading + chart (Britannica vocab)
lessons.overview: How did a food surplus from farming lead to bigger populations, new jobs, and social classes?
objectives: I can EXPLAIN how a food surplus changed society and DESCRIBE what people gained and lost, using key vocabulary and sentence starters.

lessons.title: The Story of Ogg narrative reading
lessons.overview: What did people gain and lose when they switched from hunting and gathering to farming?
objectives: I can COMPARE the lives of foragers and early farmers and EXPLAIN the tradeoffs of farming, using key vocabulary and sentence starters.

lessons.title: Paleo/Neo fill-in-the-blank review sheet
lessons.overview: How do archaeologists use evidence from Çatalhöyük to decide if it was a city or a large village?
objectives: I can DESCRIBE features of Çatalhöyük and EXPLAIN why historians disagree about it, using key vocabulary and sentence starters.

lessons.title: Early Civilizations TEST (MODS)
lessons.overview: How do I use a document and sentence frames to write a strong CRQ answer about the Neolithic Revolution as a turning point?
objectives: I can EXPLAIN why the Neolithic Revolution was a turning point and WRITE a short CRQ answer using documents and sentence frames.

units.title: River Valley Civilizations
units.blurb: The first cities and states along four rivers: Mesopotamia, Egypt, India, and China, with a vocabulary block before each one.

topics.title: Mesopotamia

lessons.title: What Makes a Civilization? (RVC Launch)
lessons.overview: What is a civilization, and why did the first ones begin near rivers in the Fertile Crescent?
objectives: Students will SAY one complete sentence using the word 'trade' to a partner, and WRITE an answer to 'How could trade help groups of people?' using the frame 'Trade could help people because ____.'

lessons.title: The Four River Valley Civilizations
lessons.overview: Where did civilizations first begin, and what are the four river valley civilizations?
objectives: Students will SAY 'The ____ river valley is in ____ (color/continent)' for each of the four valleys, and WRITE one sentence explaining how farming near a river leads to a civilization.

lessons.title: The Story of Ancient Mesopotamia (HW Reading)
lessons.overview: What did the Sumerians invent, and why was religion important in Mesopotamia?
objectives: LANGUAGE (read/write): Students will READ a simplified passage with glossed words and WRITE short answers to comprehension questions in complete sentences using the restate-the-question starter.

lessons.title: Writing Scaffold to Answering with Details
lessons.overview: How do we answer a question in a complete sentence with details?
objectives: LANGUAGE (write/say): Students will WRITE detail sentences about three pictures ('What are these people doing...?') and SAY one of their sentences to the class.

lessons.title: Mesopotamia Vocabulary (Vocab-First ①)
lessons.overview: What key words do we need to talk about Mesopotamia?
objectives: LANGUAGE (read/write): Students will READ Britannica definitions, WRITE each word's translation in their own first language in the Translate column, then WRITE 3 to 4 sentences using at least 4 of the words.

lessons.title: Mesopotamia Notes to Farming Leads to Civilization
lessons.overview: How did farming and flooding shape life in Mesopotamia?
objectives: Students will SAY advantages of living near rivers with the frame 'One advantage is ____' and WRITE the deck's fill-in blanks using yesterday's vocabulary.

lessons.title: Mesopotamia Vocabulary Recycle (Do-Now Day)
lessons.overview: How well do we remember our Mesopotamia words and facts?
objectives: LANGUAGE (read/write): Students will READ cloze sentences and WRITE the correct word-bank word in each blank; then SAY one completed sentence to a partner.

lessons.title: Mesopotamia and Hammurabi's Code
lessons.overview: Why did King Hammurabi write his laws down for everyone to see?
objectives: LANGUAGE (read/say): Students will READ the simplified Hammurabi passage with glosses ('just (fair)', 'code = law') and SAY an opinion with the frame 'I think the law is fair / not fair because ____.'

lessons.title: Code of Hammurabi to Graded Reading
lessons.overview: What do Hammurabi's laws tell us about life and trade in Babylon?
objectives: LANGUAGE (read/write): Students will READ a two-part text (background + laws) independently and WRITE complete-sentence answers for a grade, applying the restate-the-question scaffold.

lessons.title: Mesopotamia Culture to Cradle of Civilization
lessons.overview: Why is Mesopotamia called the 'Cradle of Civilization'?
objectives: LANGUAGE (read/write): Students will READ the culture passage section-by-section and WRITE a 2 to 3 sentence answer to the EQ with the frame 'Mesopotamia is called the Cradle of Civilization because ____ and ____.'

lessons.title: Mesopotamia Review Sheet (Quiz Tomorrow)
lessons.overview: How do we prepare for tomorrow's Mesopotamia quiz?
objectives: LANGUAGE (write/say): Students will WRITE definitions in their own words (with L1 support) and SAY answers during the whole-class review game.

lessons.title: Mesopotamia Quiz (Mid-Unit ⑥)
lessons.overview: What have we learned about Mesopotamia? (Quiz day)
objectives: LANGUAGE (read): Students will READ MC questions independently; question stems may be re-read aloud word-for-word on request.

lessons.title: Egypt: A Land of Achievements
lessons.overview: What achievements made Ancient Egypt one of history's most impressive civilizations?
objectives: LANGUAGE (read/write): Students will READ the achievements passage, WRITE complete-sentence answers to the do-now questions, and WRITE an opinion using 'The most impressive achievement is ____ because ____.'

lessons.title: Compare & Contrast to Mesopotamia and Egypt
lessons.overview: How were Mesopotamia and Egypt similar and different?
objectives: LANGUAGE (write): Students will WRITE a 5 to 6 sentence paragraph using compare/contrast connectors: 'Both… / However… / While Mesopotamia…, Egypt….'

lessons.title: Document Analysis to Gilgamesh and Two Afterlives
lessons.overview: What were some similarities and differences between how Mesopotamia and Egypt saw the afterlife?
objectives: LANGUAGE (read/write): Students will READ a glossed primary-source excerpt ('excerpt (part of a longer story)') and WRITE document-based answers; the do-now has them define invaders/invasion/dynasty on Britannica.

lessons.title: Indus River Valley to Geography Notes
lessons.overview: How did geography (subcontinent, mountains, monsoons) shape life in ancient India?
objectives: LANGUAGE (write/say): Students will WRITE the deck's fill-in blanks (India is a ___; the Khyber Pass is a ___) and SAY how monsoons could create problems using 'Monsoons could ____ because ____.'

lessons.title: Early China Notes to Geography and Isolation
lessons.overview: How did China's early civilizations develop, and how did geography isolate them?
objectives: LANGUAGE (write/say): Students will WRITE Student Copy fill-ins and SAY answers to the deck's thinking questions ('How could mountains benefit the people living in China?') with benefit/problem frames.

lessons.title: Thanksgiving Dinner with History (Holiday Creative Writing)
lessons.overview: Which two historical people from our year so far would you invite to Thanksgiving dinner, and what would you talk about?
objectives: LANGUAGE (write): Students will WRITE an invitation rationale and a short dialogue, practicing question forms ('What was it like to ____?') and past tense.

misconceptions: Students may read 'Fertile Crescent' as a place name only and miss that 'fertile' is an adjective (good for farming) to gloss 'fertile = good for growing' and have students translate it.
Students may answer the exit question with one word ('food'); model expanding it with the frame 'Trade could help people because they can get ____ they do not have.'
Students often think 'river valley' is the river itself; sketch valley cross-section on the board and gloss 'valley = low land beside the river.'
Color words (purple/orange/pink/yellow) may be unknown to newcomers to point at each color while saying it; allow L1 color words first.
Students may decode 'cuneiform' but think it is a thing rather than a writing SYSTEM to compare to their own alphabet/characters and to hieroglyphics later.
'Between the rivers' word order confuses some L1 grammars; draw the two rivers and physically point at the land between them.
Students may believe longer = better; show that one clear detail beats three vague words.
Some L1s drop the subject pronoun to explicitly check every sentence starts with 'The people / They.'
'Silt' and 'soil' sound alike and both relate to dirt to gloss silt as 'the GOOD mud the flood leaves behind.'
Students may translate 'surplus' as just 'more' to push for 'more than you NEED,' which matters for the civilization argument.
Students may see floods as only bad to the deck's silt slide shows floods as both gift and danger; have students say one good + one bad effect.
'Agricultural society' is abstract; gloss as 'a society where MOST people farm.'
Students may confuse the nickname 'Fertile Crescent' with 'Mesopotamia' itself to map both: crescent = the region, Mesopotamia = the land between the rivers inside it.
Matching letters (a/b/c) can be miscopied; model writing the LETTER on the line, not the whole word.
'Code' is a false friend (students think secret code) to gloss 'code can also mean LAW.'
Students may think written law automatically means fair law; tee up tomorrow's question on rich vs poor punishments.
Students may copy whole sentences from the text instead of answering the question to model finding the fact, then restating.
'Textiles' is new; gloss as 'cloth (like cotton and wool).'
'Cradle' read literally (a bed for babies) to explain the metaphor: where civilization was BORN.
Students may credit Egypt with the first writing; preview that hieroglyphics come LATER than cuneiform.
Students may study by re-reading only; model the cover-write-check routine with the index card.
'Ziggurat' vs 'pyramid' confusion starts here to gloss ziggurat as 'temple-tower with steps, for a god' before Egypt begins.
Distractor alert: Q2 offers 'hieroglyphics' for the first writing system to students who peeked ahead at Egypt may grab it; the answer is cuneiform.
Negative or 'best answer' stems are hard for ELLs; remind students to read ALL four choices before circling.
'Achievement' is abstract to gloss as 'something great that people DID or MADE.'
Students may think the pyramids were houses or temples; anchor: pyramid = tomb (using Day 13's nesting visual).
Students often list facts side by side without comparing; require connector words to force the comparison move.
'Similar' vs 'same' to gloss: similar = almost the same, with small differences.
Students assume all ancient religions imagined a happy afterlife to the Gilgamesh excerpt directly contradicts this; demand the TWO text examples.
'Excerpt' is glossed on the sheet; still verify students know they are reading PART of a longer story, not the whole epic.
Monsoon ≠ just 'storm' to it is a SEASONAL wind that brings the rain farming depends on; both halves matter.
Students may mix the Khyber Pass (a path THROUGH mountains) with the mountains themselves.
'River of Sorrows' is a nickname for the HUANG HE specifically (yellow loess soil, deadly floods) to not all Chinese rivers.
Isolation sounds purely negative; the deck asks how mountains BENEFIT China to protection is the point.
Past-tense questions ('What WAS it like') are grammatically hard; the mini-lesson exists for exactly this form.
Students may invent facts for fun to fun is allowed, but the two underlined facts must be real and traceable.

topics.title: Egypt

lessons.title: Egypt Vocabulary (Vocab-First ①)
lessons.overview: What key words do we need to talk about Ancient Egypt?
objectives: LANGUAGE (read/write): Students will READ Britannica definitions, WRITE translations in their own first language, then WRITE 4 to 5 sentences using at least 5 of the words.

lessons.title: Egypt Reading to The Gift of the Nile
lessons.overview: Why was Ancient Egypt called the 'Gift of the Nile'?
objectives: LANGUAGE (read/write): Students will READ the simplified passage and WRITE answers connecting flood → silt → food using the frame 'The flood left ____, so farmers could ____.'

lessons.title: Life in Ancient Egypt to Jobs, Pharaoh, Hieroglyphics
lessons.overview: Who did what jobs in Ancient Egypt, and who ruled everyone?
objectives: LANGUAGE (read/say): Students will READ 'Life in Ancient Egypt - part one' and SAY job descriptions with the frame 'A ____ was a person who ____.'

lessons.title: Egypt Vocabulary Do-Now / Picture Review
lessons.overview: Can we name Egypt's key people and objects from pictures alone?
objectives: LANGUAGE (write/say): Students will WRITE the correct word under each picture and SAY complete sentences from the cloze section to a partner.

lessons.title: Egypt to Pyramids, Mummies, and the Afterlife (+ Craft)
lessons.overview: Why did Egyptians build pyramids and make mummies?
objectives: LANGUAGE (read/say): Students will READ the pyramids passage (glosses: tombs = 'where important dead bodies went', afterlife = 'life after death', steal = 'take') and SAY the burial sequence using sequence words first/next/then.

lessons.title: ★ SIGNATURE PROJECT to Egyptian Mythology Instagram (Launch)
lessons.overview: How can we show an Egyptian god's powers and personality through an Instagram profile?
objectives: LANGUAGE (read/write): Students will READ god profiles from the slideshow (with pronunciation guides, e.g., Ra 'R-ah', Anubis 'Ah-noo-bus') and WRITE captions in first person ('I am Anubis. I ____.').

lessons.title: ★ Egyptian Mythology Instagram to Work Day (Due Today)
lessons.overview: How do we finish and polish our Egyptian god Instagram profiles?
objectives: LANGUAGE (write/say): Students will WRITE remaining first-person captions and SAY one finished profile aloud during the closing share.

misconceptions: 'Pharaoh' spelling/pronunciation (silent 'h' patterns) trips students to choral-say it 3 times and write the phonetic 'FAIR-oh.'
'Tomb' vs 'pyramid': the pyramid is the BUILDING, the tomb is the burial place inside to draw the nesting.
Students may think floods destroyed Egypt like the 'River of Sorrows' idea coming later in China to stress the Nile flood was predictable and GOOD.
'Highway' is figurative; gloss as 'the river worked LIKE a road for boats.'
'Priest' and 'pharaoh' both connect to religion to clarify: priests SERVED the gods; the pharaoh WAS treated as a god.
The relative clause 'a person who…' is a new structure for many; echo-correct gently and post the frame.
Papyrus vs paper: papyrus is the PLANT-made writing material to connect the words (paper comes FROM papyrus).
Scribe vs soldier images can look similar in line drawings; teach students to look for the writing tool.
'Mummy' may be known only from movies as a monster to re-anchor it as a preserved body, made out of belief in the afterlife.
Students may think every Egyptian was mummified; clarify it was pharaohs and the wealthy.
Students may invent powers from games/movies (e.g., 'Anubis the villain') to require each caption fact to trace to a slideshow slide.
First-person 'I am' captions: some students will write about the god in third person; model the switch explicitly.
Rushing students copy slide text verbatim into captions to captions must be FIRST PERSON, which forces transformation.
Some students think more gods = better grade; the rubric rewards depth on 5, not coverage of 16.

topics.title: India

lessons.title: Ancient India to Guided Reading (Vocab-in-Text)
lessons.overview: What made the early cities of Mohenjo-Daro and Harappa so advanced?
objectives: LANGUAGE (read/write): Students will READ a guided reading where key words are bolded and defined before each section, and WRITE section answers using those words.

lessons.title: Mohenjo-Daro Gallery to An Undeciphered Civilization
lessons.overview: What did archaeologists find at Harappa and Mohenjo-Daro, and what is still a mystery?
objectives: LANGUAGE (read/say): Students will READ the gallery text and SAY observations about artifact images using 'I see ____. I think it was used for ____.'

lessons.title: Hinduism to Beliefs and the Caste System
lessons.overview: What do Hindus believe about gods, reincarnation, karma, and caste?
objectives: LANGUAGE (write/say): Students will WRITE Student Copy fill-ins for the belief terms and SAY a cause-effect chain: 'If your karma is good, you ____.'

lessons.title: India Vocabulary to Cloze (Vocab ①, India-style)
lessons.overview: Can we use Hinduism's key words (caste, karma, dharma, reincarnation) correctly in a paragraph?
objectives: LANGUAGE (read/write): Students will READ the cloze paragraph about Hindu beliefs, WRITE the correct term in each blank, and WRITE translations into their own first language.

lessons.title: Ancient India Review (Assessment Tomorrow)
lessons.overview: How do we prepare for tomorrow's Ancient India assessment?
objectives: LANGUAGE (read/say): Students will READ the study guide's definitions and SAY answers in the review game in complete sentences.

lessons.title: Ancient India Assessment (⑥)
lessons.overview: What have we learned about Ancient India? (Assessment day)
objectives: LANGUAGE (read): Students will READ matching and MC items independently; stems re-read aloud on request.

lessons.title: Buddhism to The Buddha's Path
lessons.overview: How did Siddhartha Gautama become the Buddha, and what did he teach about suffering?
objectives: LANGUAGE (read/write): Students will READ the fuller Buddhism passage and WRITE answers comparing it to Monday's version ('Both readings say ____. The new reading adds ____.').

misconceptions: 'Grid' may only be known from math class; connect: streets crossing like graph-paper squares (the assessment uses the checkerboard comparison).
Students may assume ancient = primitive; the whole point is Indus plumbing was ahead of its time.
Students may say 'they had no writing' to they HAD writing; we just cannot READ it. The difference is the whole lesson.
'Archaeologist' vs 'historian': the gallery text supports glossing archaeologist as 'a person who studies things people left behind.'
Karma is NOT luck to it is earned by your actions (your deeds measure it); the cycle diagram makes this concrete.
Students may equate caste with 'job level you can change' to stress you are BORN into a caste, which Monday's cloze vocab reinforces.
Dharma (your duty) vs karma (your deed-score) reverse easily to anchor: Dharma = Do your job; Karma = Count of your good deeds.
'Polytheistic' returns from Mesopotamia to students who memorized it as 'Mesopotamian word' must see it transfers.
Subcontinent appears only in the India arc to students may blank on it; the guide's own definition ('a very large landmass that is part of a continent') is the exact assessment phrasing.
Students may skip studying matching format; remind them Part 1 is matching, worth 6 of 20 points.
MC Q7's distractors (island, peninsula, subcontinent, mountain range) are all geography words from Unit 1 to students must read all four, not stop at 'peninsula.'
On matching, students sometimes reuse a letter; remind each letter is used once.
Students may say the Buddha was a god to he was a man who became 'enlightened'; the poster reading reinforces this.
Fasting (not eating) may be confused with feasting; gloss carefully to it changes the whole story.

topics.title: China

lessons.title: China Vocabulary (Vocab-First ①)
lessons.overview: What key words do we need to talk about Ancient China?
objectives: LANGUAGE (read/write): Students will READ Britannica definitions, WRITE translations in their own first language (the teacher key models Simplified Chinese: 祖先 zǔxiān…), then WRITE 4 sentences using at least 6 of the words.

lessons.title: Oracle Bones to Make Your Own Oracle (Activity ④)
lessons.overview: How did Shang kings use oracle bones to make decisions?
objectives: LANGUAGE (write/say): Students will WRITE an oracle response (positive or negative news, warnings, advice) and SAY their oracle's message to the 'king' (partner) in future-tense sentences ('There will be ____').

lessons.title: Shang Dynasty to China's First Recorded Dynasty
lessons.overview: Why is the Shang Dynasty called China's first dynasty with written records?
objectives: LANGUAGE (read/write): Students will READ the Shang history text (with the linked intro video), WRITE the vocabulary matching (dynasty/ancestor/archaeologists), and WRITE answers citing one fact with a date.

lessons.title: Ancient China to Zhou, Qin, and Inventions
lessons.overview: What did the Zhou and Qin dynasties give China, and what did the ancient Chinese invent?
objectives: LANGUAGE (read/write): Students will READ the Ancient China passage and WRITE answers, then SAY one invention sentence: 'The ancient Chinese invented ____, which ____.'

lessons.title: Chinese Belief Systems to The Three Ways
lessons.overview: What are the 'three ways' (Buddhism, Daoism, Confucianism) that shaped Ancient China?
objectives: LANGUAGE (read/say): Students will READ the Three Ways overview and SAY the Siddhartha story in sequence using first/next/finally.

lessons.title: Confucianism to Respect, Family, and the Mandate of Heaven
lessons.overview: What did Confucius teach about family, respect, and good government?
objectives: LANGUAGE (read/write): Students will READ the Confucianism passage and WRITE answers; then WRITE one piece of Confucian advice for a modern situation using 'Confucius would say ____.'

lessons.title: ★ SIGNATURE PROJECT to Belief Systems Poster (Jigsaw Launch)
lessons.overview: How can our group teach a Chinese belief system with one clear poster?
objectives: LANGUAGE (read/write): Students will READ their group's section of the research reading and WRITE poster text in their own words to bullet points for beliefs, 2 to 3 sentences for the founder's biography.

lessons.title: ★ Belief Systems Poster to Work Day + Mini Gallery
lessons.overview: How do we finish our belief-system poster and teach it to the class?
objectives: Students will SAY a 1-minute group presentation of their poster and WRITE one fact per other system on a gallery notes sheet.

lessons.title: Ancient China Review (Test Tomorrow)
lessons.overview: How do we prepare for tomorrow's Ancient China test?
objectives: LANGUAGE (read/write/say): Students will WRITE matching letters and word-bank words, and SAY full-sentence answers in the review game.

lessons.title: Ancient China Test (MODS ⑥)
lessons.overview: What have we learned about Ancient China? (Test day)
objectives: LANGUAGE (read): Students will READ matching and fill-in items independently; the word bank reduces productive-spelling load.

misconceptions: 'Mandate' and 'heaven' are listed separately but function as ONE concept (Mandate of Heaven) to preview that next week's deck joins them.
'Ally' (friend-country/person) vs 'allegiance' (loyalty you GIVE) to the key's sample sentences disambiguate; read them aloud.
Students may think oracle bones wrote history DOWN like a diary to they were questions to ancestors/gods; the historical record is a side effect.
Future tense 'will' may be replaced with present tense by many L1 speakers; the frame bank targets exactly this.
BC dates run backwards (1600 → 1046) to physically walk the timeline to show 'bigger BC number = older.'
'First dynasty with written records' ≠ 'first people in China' to earlier people existed; records define what we KNOW.
Students may merge Shi Huangdi (Qin) with Confucius (a thinker, not an emperor) to preview Monday's belief systems to separate rulers from philosophers.
The Great Wall was built to keep INVADERS out to not to keep people in; tie back to 'invaders' from the India arc.
Buddhism STARTED in India and SPREAD to China to students often file it as 'Chinese'; the map arrow fixes this.
'Way' here means a path of thinking/living, not a road; gloss explicitly.
Confucianism is a PHILOSOPHY about behavior/government more than a religion with gods to the poster reading makes this distinction matter.
Mandate of Heaven returns from the deck to students may think Confucius INVENTED it; he explained/used the idea.
Legalism appears here for the first time (not in the week's readings) to its group needs the research reading most; T fronts them 5 extra minutes.
Groups may copy the reading verbatim to the planning frame's own-words gate exists precisely for this.
Students may study ONLY their own system to the gallery notes sheet forces all four; the China test asks about the three ways plus Legalism context.
'Impact on society' often becomes a repeat of beliefs; model the difference: belief = idea, impact = what CHANGED in China.
Loess (the yellow soil) is new-ish and easily dropped to it explains BOTH the river's name and color; rehearse the two-step.
Students may study only vocabulary; remind them Part 2 of the test is fill-in SENTENCES to practice reading whole sentences.
The 3-point barriers item needs THREE blanks (mountains + desert + the verb 'isolated') to students often fill only one; the directions phase models it.
Word-bank words are not all used to students who force every word into a blank lose points; flag this in directions.
